rows.stem:
The Cartesian equation of a line AB is :

\(\dfrac{2x - 1}{12} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{z - 3}{3}\)

Find the direction cosines of a line parallel to line AB.
rows.solution: The equation is not yet in symmetric form: the coefficient of \(x\) must be \(1\) before the denominators can be read as direction ratios. Writing \(2x - 1 = 2\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), the equation becomes \(\dfrac{2\left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)}{12} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{z - 3}{3}\), that is \(\dfrac{x - \frac{1}{2}}{6} = \dfrac{y + 2}{2} = \dfrac{z - 3}{3}\). Reading off the denominators now gives direction ratios \(6, 2, 3\), and a parallel line has the same direction ratios. To turn them into direction cosines, divide by \(\sqrt{6^2 + 2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{36 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{49} = 7\). Hence the direction cosines are \(\left\langle \dfrac{6}{7}, \dfrac{2}{7}, \dfrac{3}{7} \right\rangle\) -- or their negatives, if the line is traversed in the opposite sense. Note the trap: taking the denominators as \(12, 2, 3\) without first making the coefficient of \(x\) unity would give the wrong direction.

The limits add to \(1 + 3 = 4\), which is exactly the constant inside the second surd -- the signal to use \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(a + b - x)\,dx\). Let \(I = \int_1^{3} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{4 - x}}\,dx\) ... (1). Replacing \(x\) by \(4 - x\) swaps the two surds, giving \(I = \int_1^{3} \dfrac{\sqrt{4 - x}}{\sqrt{4 - x} + \sqrt{x}}\,dx\) ... (2). The two integrands have the same denominator and their numerators add to it, so adding (1) and (2) gives \(2I = \int_1^{3} \dfrac{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{4 - x}}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{4 - x}}\,dx = \int_1^{3} 1\,dx = \left[x\right]_1^{3} = 2\). Hence \(I = 1\).

rows.stem: Find the distance of the point \((2, 3, 4)\) measured along the line \(\dfrac{x - 4}{3} = \dfrac{y + 5}{6} = \dfrac{z + 1}{2}\) from the plane \(3x + 2y + 2z + 5 = 0\).
rows.solution: "Measured along the line" means the distance is taken along a direction parallel to the given line, not along the perpendicular to the plane -- so the perpendicular-distance formula does not apply here. Instead, draw the line through \((2, 3, 4)\) parallel to the given line and find where it meets the plane. That line is \(\dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y - 3}{6} = \dfrac{z - 4}{2}\), since a parallel line keeps the direction ratios \(3, 6, 2\). Any point on it is \((3\lambda + 2,\ 6\lambda + 3,\ 2\lambda + 4)\). Substituting into the plane, \(3(3\lambda + 2) + 2(6\lambda + 3) + 2(2\lambda + 4) + 5 = 0\), that is \(9\lambda + 6 + 12\lambda + 6 + 4\lambda + 8 + 5 = 0\), so \(25\lambda + 25 = 0\) and \(\lambda = -1\). The point of intersection is therefore \((-1, -3, 2)\). The required distance is the distance from \((2, 3, 4)\) to \((-1, -3, 2)\), namely \(\sqrt{(2 + 1)^2 + (3 + 3)^2 + (4 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} = \sqrt{49} = 7\) units.

rows.stem: There are two boxes, namely box-I and box-II. Box-I contains 3 red and 6 black balls. Box-II contains 5 red and 5 black balls. One of the two boxes, is selected at random and a ball is drawn at random. The ball drawn is found to be red. Find the probability that this red ball comes out from box-II.
rows.solution: The colour is observed and the box is to be inferred, so this is Bayes' theorem. Let \(E_1\) be the event that box-I is selected, \(E_2\) that box-II is selected, and \(A\) that the ball drawn is red. A box is chosen at random, so \(P(E_1) = P(E_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Box-I holds 3 red out of \(3 + 6 = 9\) balls, so \(P(A \mid E_1) = \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{1}{3}\); box-II holds 5 red out of \(5 + 5 = 10\), so \(P(A \mid E_2) = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). By Bayes' theorem, \(P(E_2 \mid A) = \dfrac{P(E_2)P(A \mid E_2)}{P(E_1)P(A \mid E_1) + P(E_2)P(A \mid E_2)}\). Every term carries the common factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) for the box choice, which cancels, leaving \(P(E_2 \mid A) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{5}{6}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}\). Hence the probability that the red ball came from box-II is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\), which is above \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) as expected, since box-II is the richer source of red balls.
